definition: The Zeuthen strategy in cognitive science is a negotiation strategy used by some artificial agents.
details: Its purpose is to measure the willingness to risk conflict. An agent will be more willing to risk conflict if it does not have much to lose in case that the negotiation fails. In contrast, an agent is less willing to risk conflict when it has more to lose. The value of a deal is expressed in its utility. An agent has much to lose when the difference between the utility of its current proposal and the conflict deal is high. When both agents use the monotonic concession protocol, the Zeuthen strategy leads them to agree upon a deal in the negotiation set. This set consists of all conflict free deals, which are individually rational and Pareto optimal, and the conflict deal, which maximizes the Nash product. The strategy was introduced in 1930 by the Danish economist Frederik Zeuthen.

explainer.lead: The Zeuthen strategy is a negotiation strategy used by some artificial agents to measure willingness to risk conflict. An agent with little to lose from failure is more willing to risk conflict than one with much to lose.

tiers.eli5: Like a haggler who pushes harder when walking away costs them little, and backs down when a failed deal would hurt them a lot.
tiers.practitioner: Agents using it gauge risk willingness from the gap between their current proposal's utility and the conflict deal, and it pairs with the monotonic concession protocol. A pitfall is that concessions depend on accurately valuing that gap.
tiers.paperLevel: An agent has much to lose when the difference between the utility of its current proposal and the conflict deal is high, making it less willing to risk conflict; the strategy is used with the monotonic concession protocol.

explainer.example: An agent whose current proposal offers utility far above the conflict deal is less willing to risk conflict and concedes accordingly.
